subject: ela
skillName: Ask and answer questions about a speaker

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Birds migrate in winter.' You do not know what 'migrate' means. Which clarifying question is best?
A) 'Do you like birds?'
B) 'What does migrate mean?'
C) 'Can we go outside?'

steps: Asking for the meaning of a word you don't understand is a clarifying question that helps comprehension.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Dolphins are very smart animals.' You want more information. Which question gathers additional information?
A) 'How smart are dolphins compared to other animals?'
B) 'What is your name?'
C) 'Do dolphins have fins?'
items.answer: A) 'How smart are dolphins compared to other animals?'

steps: 'How smart compared to other animals?' asks for additional specific information that expands on the speaker's vague claim ('very smart').

items.prompt:
After a speaker's talk, a student is asked: 'What did the speaker say about honey bees?' The student answers: 'The speaker said honey bees make honey by collecting nectar and mixing it with enzymes in the hive.' Is this a strong answer?
A) No — it is too long
B) Yes — it includes specific details about the process the speaker described
C) No — the student should have only said 'bees make honey'
items.answer: B) Yes — it includes specific details about the process the speaker described

steps: A strong answer about what a speaker said includes the process (collecting nectar, mixing with enzymes) — not just the outcome (bees make honey).

items.prompt:
A teacher explains: 'The heart pumps blood to every part of the body.' A student asks: 'Does the heart pump blood to the brain too?' What type of question is this?
A) A question that changes the topic to the brain
B) A question that deepens understanding by asking about a specific application of the speaker's statement
C) A question that disagrees with the teacher
items.answer: B) A question that deepens understanding by asking about a specific application of the speaker's statement

steps: The teacher said 'every part' — the student is asking whether that includes the brain.
This is not a topic change — it stays on the heart and its function.
Asking 'does this include X?' deepens understanding of the scope of the claim.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Ancient Greeks invented many things we still use today.' A student asks: 'What are two specific inventions from ancient Greece that we still use?' Why is this a good question?
A) It is not good — it asks for specifics
B) It gathers additional information by asking the speaker to name specific examples of the vague phrase 'many things'
C) It is only good if the student likes history
items.answer: B) It gathers additional information by asking the speaker to name specific examples of the vague phrase 'many things'

steps: 'Many things' is vague — the student wants specific examples.
Asking for two specific examples makes the speaker's claim concrete and verifiable.
This is a strong information-gathering question.

items.prompt:
A student hears a speaker and is asked: 'What question would you ask to deepen your understanding of this topic?' The speaker said: 'Trees help reduce pollution in cities.' The student's best question is:
A) 'How do trees reduce pollution — what actually happens?'
B) 'Are there trees in your yard?'
C) 'What city do you live in?'
items.answer: A) 'How do trees reduce pollution — what actually happens?'

steps: The speaker stated the WHAT (trees reduce pollution) but not the HOW (the mechanism).
Asking 'how does it actually happen?' deepens understanding by asking for the process behind the claim.
Options B and C are personal questions unrelated to understanding the topic.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Planting trees can help fight climate change.' A student asks: 'If planting trees helps, why is climate change still getting worse?' Evaluate this question.
A) Weak — it challenges the speaker and is disrespectful
B) Strong — it asks for clarification of an apparent contradiction, which deepens understanding of both why trees help AND why they may not be enough
C) Weak — it asks about a different topic (why climate change is worsening)
items.answer: B) Strong — it asks for clarification of an apparent contradiction, which deepens understanding of both why trees help AND why they may not be enough

steps: The student notices a seeming contradiction: if trees help, why is the problem worsening?
This is not disrespectful — it is intellectually honest engagement with the claim.
The answer would explain that planting trees helps but other factors (emissions, deforestation rates) outpace the benefit.
Questions that probe apparent contradictions are among the most powerful for deepening understanding.

items.prompt:
A student listened carefully to a speaker's presentation about the solar system. Afterward, the teacher asks: 'What did the speaker say, and what question would you still ask?' The student responds: 'The speaker said there are eight planets in our solar system, and each one has a different size, distance from the sun, and composition. I would still ask: has any planet besides Earth ever had liquid water, since water is needed for life?' Evaluate this full response.
A) Weak — the student asked a question the speaker already answered
B) Strong — the student accurately recounted key facts (eight planets, differences) and asked a specific, logical follow-up question not covered in the talk
C) Adequate — but the student's question is too advanced
items.answer: B) Strong — the student accurately recounted key facts (eight planets, differences) and asked a specific, logical follow-up question not covered in the talk

steps: Part 1 (recounting): 'eight planets, different size/distance/composition' — specific and accurate.
Part 2 (follow-up question): 'has any planet besides Earth ever had liquid water?' — specific, logical, and relevant.
The follow-up connects to something the speaker mentioned (planets) and extends toward a new topic (life/water) — deepening understanding.
This is a model two-part response demonstrating both answering and asking skills.
